136	**Couldn't judge from a still.** Only items that matter for this piece. Omit if none.
137	
138	**Checklist.** One line per section, each on its own line, with your final answers: `Text: 30 lines, 27 yes, 2 no (body text large enough; lines of 45 to 75 characters), 1 unsure (space between lines)`, or `Charts and data: skipped`. Do not repeat the walk here.
139	```

153	- [ ] **Does each control sit next to the thing it changes?** → `references/ux.md` "Norman: Natural mapping"
154	- [ ] **Is the form one column, with fields side by side only for short related pairs?** → `references/ux.md` "Forms: single column layout" _(off-list source)_
155	- [ ] **Are required or optional fields marked?** → `references/ux.md` "Forms: inline validation and required markers"
156	- [ ] **Is each error stated in words that name the field, not shown by color or an icon alone?** → `references/accessibility.md` "Error identification"; `references/ux.md` "Error states"; `references/ux.md` "Nielsen 9: Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors"
157	- [ ] **Does each error message say how to correct it?** → `references/accessibility.md` "Error suggestion"
158	- [ ] **Does an empty list or dashboard tell the user what to do next?** → `references/ux.md` "Empty states"
159	- [ ] **Where the task is complex, is short help shown near the step it concerns?** → `references/ux.md` "Nielsen 10: Help and documentation"
160	- [ ] **Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?** → `references/ux.md` "Nielsen 7: Flexibility and efficiency of use"; `references/ux.md` "Shneiderman: Enable frequent users to use shortcuts" _(off-list source)_
161	- [ ] **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them (a prefilled default, the next action, or the information they came for) instead of making them hunt for it?** → `references/ux.md` "Tognazzini: Anticipation" _(off-list source)_
162	- [ ] **Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products?** → `references/ux.md` "Jakob's law"; `references/ux.md` "Platform conventions (Apple HIG and Material)"
163	- [ ] **Do labels and messages use the audience's own words rather than internal or system terms?** → `references/ux.md` "Nielsen 2: Match between system and the real world"
164	- [ ] **Can each link's purpose be told from its text or the sentence around it?** → `references/accessibility.md` "Link purpose (in context)"

content.content:
=== references/accessibility.md
### Reflow

- **Rule:** At a 320 CSS px wide viewport (400% zoom of 1280 px) content reflows to one column with no horizontal scrolling and no loss of information. Exceptions: data tables, maps, diagrams, video, and toolbars needing two-dimensional layout; vertical content uses 256 CSS px height.
- **Source:** WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10 (AA)
- **Link:** https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/reflow.html
- **Caveat:** breaks NG-10 because it needs a render at 320 px wide, which one image cannot show.

=== references/ux.md
### Primary versus secondary action

- **Rule:** One primary action per view is visually dominant (filled, high contrast); secondary actions are lower emphasis (outline or text); cancel and tertiary actions are weakest. Two equal-weight filled buttons is a fault.
- **Source:** Material Design 3, "Buttons" guidance (emphasis levels); Apple HIG, "Buttons"; NN/g, "Visual Hierarchy" and "Button Design" guidance.
- **Link:** https://m3.material.io/components/buttons/guidelines

=== references/basics.md
### Secondary actions are not styled as strongly as the primary one

- **Rule:** A view has one high-emphasis action. Other actions use lower-emphasis styles, such as outlined or text buttons.
- **Look for:** Are two or more buttons in one view styled as the same filled, high-emphasis button?
- **Source:** Material Design 3, "Buttons" guidelines: "Use visually-prominent filled buttons for the most important actions", and "Buttons with primary actions should have a higher visual emphasis through size, color, or shape." Checked on the rendered page on 2026-10-24.
- **Link:** https://m3.material.io/components/buttons/guidelines
- **Fix (approved), Secondary actions are styled as strongly as the primary one:** Give the view one high-emphasis action, and style the other actions with lower-emphasis styles, such as outlined or text buttons (Material Design 3, "Buttons").
- **How bad it gets:** not measured. Two or more buttons in one view with the same filled, high-emphasis style.

=== references/accessibility.md
### Non-text contrast

- **Rule:** Visual boundaries needed to identify a UI component need at least 3:1 against adjacent colors: an input border, a checkbox, a button edge when there is no other cue. So do meaningful graphics such as chart lines and icons that carry meaning. Also applies to focus and selected states.
- **Source:** WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11 (AA)
- **Link:** https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/non-text-contrast.html
- **Caveat:** `non-text-contrast-faint` was cut after the pre-screen (crit-q25.17), with pre-screen figures 0.42, 0.12 / 0.10, 0.11. Jev stayed quiet on a clear positive.

=== references/color.md
### Non-text contrast

- **Rule:** UI component boundaries and states (input borders, icons that carry meaning, focus rings) and meaningful chart graphics are at least 3:1 against adjacent colors.
- **Source:** W3C, *WCAG 2.2*, Success Criterion 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (2023)
- **Link:** https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#non-text-contrast

=== references/typography.md
### Sizes come from a scale

- **Rule:** Text sizes come from a small, deliberate scale, so that each size reads as its own level. Many sizes that are almost the same show that sizes were picked one at a time.
- **Look for:** Are there two blocks of ordinary paragraph text, in the same typeface and weight and with no heading role, where the letters of one block are a little larger than the letters of the other, so that the two blocks do not match when seen side by side or one after the other?
- **Source:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, section 3.1.1 "Don't compose without a scale", p. 45 (from the scan's OCR text): "limit yourself, at first, to a modest set of distinct and related intervals."

=== references/art-direction.md
### Visual hierarchy has distinct levels

- **Rule:** There are two to four clearly different levels of importance, and each level is distinguishable from the next at a glance.
- **Source:** Josef Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design* (1981); Ellen Lupton and Jennifer Cole Phillips, *Graphic Design: The New Basics* (2008).

=== references/accessibility.md
### Text contrast (minimum)

- **Rule:** Body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background; large text (at least 24 CSS px, or 18.66 CSS px bold) needs at least 3:1. Logos and disabled controls are exempt.
- **Source:** WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3 (AA)
- **Link:** https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html
- **Caveat:** the basics criterion `text-reads-faint` asks it, and a rule has one owner, so the accessibility pack does not ask it again.

=== references/typography.md
### Line length (measure)

- **Rule:** A single column of paragraph text must not run so wide that the eye loses its place on the way back to the start of the next line. Bringhurst gives 45 to 75 characters as the comfortable range, 66 as the ideal, and 40 to 50 for text set in several columns.
- **Look for:** Does a paragraph of body text stretch in one column from the left margin of the page to the right margin, with no sidebar, image, or second column beside it, so that its lines are as wide as the page's content area?
- **Source:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style* (Version 3.0, 2004), section 2.1.2 "Choose a comfortable measure", p. 26 (from the scan's OCR text): "Anything from 45 to 75 characters is widely regarded as a satisfactory length of line for a single-column page".

=== references/typography.md
### Line breaks in headings and short text

- **Rule:** Headings, buttons, and captions break at natural phrase boundaries and do not split a word, a number and its unit, or a name across lines.
- **Source:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, section 2.4 "Etiquette of hyphenation and pagination", section 2.4.6 (link short numerical expressions with hard spaces), which supports a number and its unit; Hochuli, *Detail in Typography* (2008). UNVERIFIED: breaks in headings were not found in Bringhurst or in Hochuli.
- **Caveat:** it reads the words to judge where a line breaks, which is the content.

=== references/typography.md
### Widows, orphans, and runts

- **Rule:** A paragraph does not end with one short word alone on its last line, and a column does not begin with the last line of a paragraph. A heading does not sit at the foot of a column with its text in the next one.
- **Source:** Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, sections 2.4.2 (no short last-line word) and 2.4.8 (never begin a page with the last line of a paragraph). Both are supported. UNVERIFIED: a heading at the foot of a column was not found in Bringhurst.

=== references/layout.md
### One grid governs the page

- **Rule:** Every block takes its edges from one underlying grid of columns, margins, and intervals, so the same column lines recur from the top of the page to the bottom. A block whose edges match no other block shows that it was placed by eye.
- **Look for:** Does one block look out of line with the rest of the page, as if it were placed by eye and not on the same columns as the blocks around it?
- **Source:** Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design* (1981), sections "Grid and design philosophy" and "Construction of the grid"; Samara, *Making and Breaking the Grid* (3rd ed. 2023), part "Making the Grid".

=== references/layout.md
### White space is gathered, not scattered

- **Rule:** Ruder holds that the printed and the unprinted areas must stand in tension, and that the tension comes from contrast. Considered work gathers empty space into a few large, shaped areas set against dense ones. Average work spreads the same small gap between everything, so no space does any work, and it runs content up to the edges of the page.
- **Look for:** Does the page look evenly filled, with its empty space spread thin between everything and no open area large enough to give the eye a place to rest?
- **Source:** Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design* (1967), chapters "Contrasts" and "Form and counter-form"; Kunz, *Typography: Macro- and Microaesthetics* (1998), part two, on space and on form and counterform.

=== references/layout.md
### Balance

- **Rule:** Visual weight comes from size, darkness, color, and isolation, and where an element sits changes its weight. A layout may be symmetrical or not, but a heavy side needs a counterweight.
- **Look for:** Does one side of the page carry much more visual weight than the other, with nothing on the lighter side strong enough to balance it?
- **Source:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, chapter I "Balance", sections "Weight" and "Psychological and physical balance".

**First read.** On desktop the eye lands on the headline, "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks", and then crosses to the "Reorder this week" table. From there it is pulled up to the rust "Sign in" button, the only filled, colored thing on the page. The real offer, "Start a 30-day trial", is a beige box that reads as a second choice. The page feels quiet, plain, and specific to bookshops. On the phone and tablet the layout does not stack. The headline is squeezed into a narrow column seven lines tall, the table runs off the right edge, and the page scrolls sideways.

**What it's for.** A landing page that persuades independent bookshop owners to start a trial of Shelfmark, stock-tracking software.

**Verdict.** The message is right, and the table is good proof of it. Two things get in the way. On a phone the page is broken, and on every screen the loudest button sends visitors to "Sign in" instead of to the trial.

**What would move it most**

1. **The layout does not collapse on narrow screens.** The page renders 789 px wide at both the 390 px phone and the 768 px tablet widths (`page_width`), so both scroll sideways. On the phone, the hero text and the table stay side by side. This causes several problems:
   - The headline wraps to 7 lines at 6.8 characters per line (`h1`).
   - The table starts at x=310 and runs past the screen edge.
   - Both buttons wrap to 3 or 4 lines and split "30-/day" across lines.
   - "Shops using it" breaks onto 3 lines and "Sign in" onto 2.
   - The three facts at the bottom shrink to about 5 characters per line (`section.facts > p`), which makes a staircase rag.
   - The header rule stops at 390 px.

   Many bookshop owners will first open this page from a link on their phone. What they see looks broken, and a product that promises to keep order does not get that first impression back. Defect, WCAG 1.4.10 (Reflow). Fix: below a tablet width, stack everything in one column: headline, paragraph, buttons, table, then the facts one under another. Let the table use the full width, and keep the buttons on one line each. Viewports: phone, tablet

2. **The strongest button is the one new visitors don't need.** "Sign in" is the only filled, saturated button (white on #8a3b24, weight 500). "Start a 30-day trial" is weight 400 gray text on a beige fill (#f3eee6) that barely separates from the cream page (#fffdf9). Next to "See how it works" it looks like the same weight of button. The result is that a first-time visitor's eye goes to the exit meant for existing customers, and the trial looks optional. Convention, Material Design 3 "Buttons": one high-emphasis action per view. Fix: give the trial the rust fill and the heavier weight. Bring "Sign in" down to an outlined button or a plain nav link like its neighbors. Leave "See how it works" as the outlined secondary. Viewports: all

3. **The copy states what the product does but not whether it works for this shop.** Two lines are the problem:
   - "Works with your till" is the line a bookshop owner checks first, and it doesn't say which tills or card readers. An owner whose till isn't named will assume it's not supported. Name the kind of fact that is missing, the list of supported tills or card readers, and leave the list itself to the maker.
   - "Returns tracked." has no verb and stops at the fact. Who tracks them, and what does it save the owner? The line should end on what the date list means for the owner, said to "you". The current wording leaves the owner to work that out.

   Beyond those two lines, the page never compares Shelfmark with what the owner does now, such as walking the shelves on Monday or reading the till's own sales report. That comparison would let them judge the value themselves. Say what kind of comparison would help and leave the maker to write it. Defect for the till line, which decides whether an owner can use the product at all; taste for the rest. Viewports: all

4. **On widescreen, the headline and its proof sit about 770 px apart.** The hero text keeps to the left edge (x=64 to 604), and the table moves out to x=1377. The table is the proof of the headline, but here it reads as a separate widget across an empty field, and the eye has to travel the full width to connect them. Convention, proximity (`Space shows the groups`): the space inside a group should be smaller than the space between groups. Here the gap inside the hero is far larger than the gap from the hero to the facts below it. Fix: cap the width of the content area, or keep the table at a fixed distance from the text, so the pair stays together as the screen gets wider. Viewports: widescreen

**Smaller things.**
- The table column headers ("Title", "On shelf", "Sold this week") and the date "Mon 9 June" are #8a8178 on white, which is 3.82:1 (`contrast`, `thead > tr > th`, `span.preview-date`) and under the 4.5:1 minimum. Darken them to the body gray #5c544b, which still reads as secondary. Viewports: all
- There are five type sizes, 40, 20, 16, 15, and 14 px (`type_sizes`). The steps 16, 15, and 14 are too close to read as levels. Fold them into one body size and one small size, and use weight or color for the rest (Bringhurst 3.1.1). Viewports: all
- The headline leaves "asks" alone on its third line, which splits the phrase "a customer asks". A slightly narrower or wider measure would break it after "shelves". Viewports: desktop, widescreen
- The fact lines run to 79 and 81 characters (`characters_per_line`, `section.facts > p`), which is long for one of three columns, and "take." sits alone on the second line of the middle fact. Narrow the columns. Viewports: widescreen
- The page ends at about y=548, and the bottom third of the desktop screen is empty. Nothing below the facts follows up on the nav links "Pricing" and "Shops using it". Viewports: desktop, widescreen

**What's working.**
- The "Reorder this week" table is the best thing on the page. It uses plausible titles, a real date, and the two numbers an owner thinks in ("On shelf" and "Sold this week"), so the product shows its output instead of only describing it. Keep it as the main image.
- The headline is in the owner's own words and names a moment they know, a customer asking for a book. The paragraph under it says exactly what happens and when ("on Monday morning").
- The palette is small and warm, with readable body text: 7.32:1 contrast and 68 characters per line on desktop (`div.hero-text > p`). It has no template gloss, so the page looks made for this audience.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Hover and focus states on the three buttons. They matter most for the beige trial button, whose resting state is already faint.
- Whether "Pricing" and "Shops using it" link to content. Neither section appears on the captured page.

**Checklist.**
The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes
What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (distinct text levels)
Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (space inside groups smaller than between groups; margin from screen edge)
Text: 30 lines, 25 yes, 5 no (text contrast; line length; rag; widows and runts; line breaks in headings and buttons)
Color: 9 lines, 9 yes
Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes
Charts and data: 16 lines, 16 yes
Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (one primary action; reflow), 3 unsure (hover and pressed states; focus indicator; focus not obscured)
Template tells: 10 lines, 10 yes

1	# Where it could go further
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A critic has already written a crit of a design. Your one job is to write the section "Where it could go further": what a stronger version of this piece would commit to, beyond fixing what the crit found. You do not change the crit, edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the image whole. When your prompt names several images, they are one page at several viewports, not versions: read each one, and build on the page as a whole. Look closely at anything you build an idea on. If the image is taller than one screen, you may run `node scripts/crop.mjs <in.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops it prints, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run it as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
12	2. Read the crit file. Note what it says the piece is for, every item under "What would move it most" with its number, and every item under "Smaller things".
13	3. Write the section by the rules below.
14	
15	## The rules
16	
17	- **Up to three numbered commitments** a stronger version of this piece would make. Fewer items are fine.
18	- **Each one starts from a specific element of this piece and names it.** Suggest that the piece own one color, let one number lead, or commit to one typeface only when that color, number, or typeface is already in the piece.
19	- **Each one names what the piece is for and how the commitment serves that.** Take the purpose from the crit's "What it's for".
20	- **Each one is marked taste and argues for itself.** Cite a source from the list in `agents/critic.md` under "Sources you may cite" when one states the idea, by author and work or by standard and number. Never invent a source or a figure.
21	- **Direction, not redesign.** Say what the commitment is and why, and leave the design to the designer.
22	- **Nothing repeated.** Before you write an item, check it against the ranked list and "Smaller things". When it grows out of a finding, start it with "Builds on finding N", where N is that finding's number in "What would move it most", and give only the new commitment. When nothing new is left, drop the item.
23	- **Nothing beyond the findings.** When the findings already say it all, write "Nothing beyond the findings." as the whole body of the section.

25	- **Plain language.** Talk like a sharp designer across a table from a peer. No jargon you would not say aloud, no hedging. Write US spelling (color, center, gray, organize).
26	
27	## What you return
28	
29	Your final message is the section and nothing else: no preface, no other heading, no copy of the crit. It starts with the bold heading on its own line.

33	1. <Commitment>: the element it starts from, what it commits to, how that serves what the piece is for, marked taste, with a source if one states it.
34	2. ...
35	```

40	**Where it could go further.** Nothing beyond the findings.
41	```

summary:
**Where it could go further.**
1. **Let the empty shelves lead the table.** Two rows in "Reorder this week" show 0 in "On shelf": "A Year of Hedges" and "The Glass Orchard". Those zeros are the exact moment the headline names, a customer asking for a book the shop no longer has. Right now they get the same plain weight as every other cell, so a visitor has to read every number to find the point. A stronger version would make the zero-stock rows the first thing the eye finds in the table, through weight or a tint taken from the existing warm palette. Use the color sparingly so it doesn't compete with the trial button once that button takes the rust fill. This serves the page's job directly: the owner sees the problem the product solves before reading a word of the pitch. Taste. Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, argues that the ink in a display should show the data that matters, and here the data that matters is the zeros.
2. **Make the page about one Monday.** The paragraph promises a reorder list "on Monday morning", and the table is dated "Mon 9 June". Those are the same moment, but the page presents them as two separate things: a sentence on the left and a widget on the right. A stronger version would commit to that Monday as the idea that ties the page together, so the table reads as the list the owner gets that morning and the paragraph reads as its caption. The owner is buying a routine, not a database. A page that shows one concrete Monday of that routine makes the trial feel like a small, known step rather than a software purchase. This is a matter of framing and of how close the two pieces sit together, not of new copy. Taste. Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*, argues that a page should make what it offers obvious at a glance, and here one familiar moment does that better than a list of features.

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.
78

1	**First read.** On desktop the eye lands on the headline, "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks", and then crosses to the "Reorder this week" table. From there it is pulled up to the rust "Sign in" button, the only filled, colored thing on the page. The real offer, "Start a 30-day trial", is a beige box that reads as a second choice. The page feels quiet, plain, and specific to bookshops. On the phone and tablet the layout does not stack. The headline is squeezed into a narrow column seven lines tall, the table runs off the right edge, and the page scrolls sideways.
2	
3	**What it's for.** A landing page that persuades independent bookshop owners to start a trial of Shelfmark, stock-tracking software.
4	
5	**Verdict.** The message is right, and the table is good proof of it. Two things get in the way. On a phone the page is broken, and on every screen the loudest button sends visitors to "Sign in" instead of to the trial.
6	
7	**What would move it most**
8	
9	1. **The layout does not collapse on narrow screens.** The page renders 789 px wide at both the 390 px phone and the 768 px tablet widths (`page_width`), so both scroll sideways. On the phone, the hero text and the table stay side by side. This causes several problems:
10	   - The headline wraps to 7 lines at 6.8 characters per line (`h1`).
11	   - The table starts at x=310 and runs past the screen edge.
12	   - Both buttons wrap to 3 or 4 lines and split "30-/day" across lines.
13	   - "Shops using it" breaks onto 3 lines and "Sign in" onto 2.
14	   - The three facts at the bottom shrink to about 5 characters per line (`section.facts > p`), which makes a staircase rag.
15	   - The header rule stops at 390 px.
16	
17	   Many bookshop owners will first open this page from a link on their phone. What they see looks broken, and a product that promises to keep order does not get that first impression back. Defect, WCAG 1.4.10 (Reflow). Fix: below a tablet width, stack everything in one column: headline, paragraph, buttons, table, then the facts one under another. Let the table use the full width, and keep the buttons on one line each. Viewports: phone, tablet
18	
19	2. **The strongest button is the one new visitors don't need.** "Sign in" is the only filled, saturated button (white on #8a3b24, weight 500). "Start a 30-day trial" is weight 400 gray text on a beige fill (#f3eee6) that barely separates from the cream page (#fffdf9). Next to "See how it works" it looks like the same weight of button. The result is that a first-time visitor's eye goes to the exit meant for existing customers, and the trial looks optional. Convention, Material Design 3 "Buttons": one high-emphasis action per view. Fix: give the trial the rust fill and the heavier weight. Bring "Sign in" down to an outlined button or a plain nav link like its neighbors. Leave "See how it works" as the outlined secondary. Viewports: all
20	
21	3. **The copy states what the product does but not whether it works for this shop.** Two lines are the problem:
22	   - "Works with your till" is the line a bookshop owner checks first, and it doesn't say which tills or card readers. An owner whose till isn't named will assume it's not supported. Name the kind of fact that is missing, the list of supported tills or card readers, and leave the list itself to the maker.
23	   - "Returns tracked." has no verb and stops at the fact. Who tracks them, and what does it save the owner? The line should end on what the date list means for the owner, said to "you". The current wording leaves the owner to work that out.
24	
25	   Beyond those two lines, the page never compares Shelfmark with what the owner does now, such as walking the shelves on Monday or reading the till's own sales report. That comparison would let them judge the value themselves. Say what kind of comparison would help and leave the maker to write it. Defect for the till line, which decides whether an owner can use the product at all; taste for the rest. Viewports: all
26	
27	4. **On widescreen, the headline and its proof sit about 770 px apart.** The hero text keeps to the left edge (x=64 to 604), and the table moves out to x=1377. The table is the proof of the headline, but here it reads as a separate widget across an empty field, and the eye has to travel the full width to connect them. Convention, proximity (`Space shows the groups`): the space inside a group should be smaller than the space between groups. Here the gap inside the hero is far larger than the gap from the hero to the facts below it. Fix: cap the width of the content area, or keep the table at a fixed distance from the text, so the pair stays together as the screen gets wider. Viewports: widescreen
28	
29	**Smaller things.**
30	- The table column headers ("Title", "On shelf", "Sold this week") and the date "Mon 9 June" are #8a8178 on white, which is 3.82:1 (`contrast`, `thead > tr > th`, `span.preview-date`) and under the 4.5:1 minimum. Darken them to the body gray #5c544b, which still reads as secondary. Viewports: all
31	- There are five type sizes, 40, 20, 16, 15, and 14 px (`type_sizes`). The steps 16, 15, and 14 are too close to read as levels. Fold them into one body size and one small size, and use weight or color for the rest (Bringhurst 3.1.1). Viewports: all
32	- The headline leaves "asks" alone on its third line, which splits the phrase "a customer asks". A slightly narrower or wider measure would break it after "shelves". Viewports: desktop, widescreen
33	- The fact lines run to 79 and 81 characters (`characters_per_line`, `section.facts > p`), which is long for one of three columns, and "take." sits alone on the second line of the middle fact. Narrow the columns. Viewports: widescreen
34	- The page ends at about y=548, and the bottom third of the desktop screen is empty. Nothing below the facts follows up on the nav links "Pricing" and "Shops using it". Viewports: desktop, widescreen
35	
36	**What's working.**
37	- The "Reorder this week" table is the best thing on the page. It uses plausible titles, a real date, and the two numbers an owner thinks in ("On shelf" and "Sold this week"), so the product shows its output instead of only describing it. Keep it as the main image.
38	- The headline is in the owner's own words and names a moment they know, a customer asking for a book. The paragraph under it says exactly what happens and when ("on Monday morning").
39	- The palette is small and warm, with readable body text: 7.32:1 contrast and 68 characters per line on desktop (`div.hero-text > p`). It has no template gloss, so the page looks made for this audience.
40	
41	**Where it could go further.**
42	1. **Let the empty shelves lead the table.** Two rows in "Reorder this week" show 0 in "On shelf": "A Year of Hedges" and "The Glass Orchard". Those zeros are the exact moment the headline names, a customer asking for a book the shop no longer has. Right now they get the same plain weight as every other cell, so a visitor has to read every number to find the point. A stronger version would make the zero-stock rows the first thing the eye finds in the table, through weight or a tint taken from the existing warm palette. Use the color sparingly so it doesn't compete with the trial button once that button takes the rust fill. This serves the page's job directly: the owner sees the problem the product solves before reading a word of the pitch. Taste. Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, argues that the ink in a display should show the data that matters, and here the data that matters is the zeros.
43	2. **Make the page about one Monday.** The paragraph promises a reorder list "on Monday morning", and the table is dated "Mon 9 June". Those are the same moment, but the page presents them as two separate things: a sentence on the left and a widget on the right. A stronger version would commit to that Monday as the idea that ties the page together, so the table reads as the list the owner gets that morning and the paragraph reads as its caption. The owner is buying a routine, not a database. A page that shows one concrete Monday of that routine makes the trial feel like a small, known step rather than a software purchase. This is a matter of framing and of how close the two pieces sit together, not of new copy. Taste. Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*, argues that a page should make what it offers obvious at a glance, and here one familiar moment does that better than a list of features.
44	
45	**Couldn't judge from a still.**
46	- Hover and focus states on the three buttons. They matter most for the beige trial button, whose resting state is already faint.
47	- Whether "Pricing" and "Shops using it" link to content. Neither section appears on the captured page.
48	
49	**Checklist.**
50	The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes
51	What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (distinct text levels)
52	Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (space inside groups smaller than between groups; margin from screen edge)
53	Text: 30 lines, 25 yes, 5 no (text contrast; line length; rag; widows and runts; line breaks in headings and buttons)
54	Color: 9 lines, 9 yes
55	Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes
56	Charts and data: 16 lines, 16 yes
57	Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (one primary action; reflow), 3 unsure (hover and pressed states; focus indicator; focus not obscured)
58	Template tells: 10 lines, 10 yes
59

content.content:
1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and the fix added no template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but the element the fix added is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the after image has and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background, as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. A new element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and the element the fix added is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.

summary:
**First read.** The eye lands on the headline "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks". It then drops to the rust "Start a 30-day trial" button and crosses to the "Reorder this week" table. The page reads as a calm, plain product page for an independent bookshop's stock tool: warm off-white, one rust accent, and a real-looking table as proof. On tablet and phone everything stacks in one column in a sensible order: headline, paragraph, buttons, table, then the three fact lines. Nothing scrolls sideways.

**What it's for.** It gets an independent bookshop owner to start a 30-day trial of Shelfmark, the stock-counting and reorder tool.

**Verdict.** The fixes worked. The page now reflows on narrow screens, the trial is the one strong button, and the hero holds together on widescreen. What still stands between the page and a sign-up is copy only the maker can supply: which tills it works with, how it compares with the owner's Monday routine, and a section that answers the Pricing and "Shops using it" links.

**Finding status**
- no-reflow-narrow-screens: closed. page_width is 390 on the phone and 768 on the tablet, and the phone h1 is 3 lines at 18 characters per line. The content is in one column and each button is on one line.
- sign-in-outshouts-trial: closed. In all viewports, Sign in is a plain nav link (weight 500, #2a2622), and "Start a 30-day trial" is the only filled button (white on #8a3b24, 7.69:1).
- copy-misses-fit-for-this-shop: open. The returns line now has a verb and speaks to the owner ("Tracks your returns. You see which unsold copies are due back, and when."). The till line still names no tills or card readers, and the page still has no comparison with what the owner does now.
- widescreen-hero-gap: closed. The h1 right edge is at x=984 and the table text starts at x=1075, about 91 px apart, inside the check's 200 px. The content is capped at 384 to 1536.
- faint-table-headers: closed. The headers and "Mon 9 June" measure 7.43:1, and violations is empty in all viewports.
- too-many-close-type-sizes: open, but only just. type_sizes is now 40 (32 on phone), 20, 16, 14, which meets the target of one body size and one small size. But 16 and 14 are exactly 2 px apart, which the "within 2 px" check catches.
- headline-lone-word: closed. On desktop and widescreen the headline is 2 lines and breaks after "shelves", so "before a customer asks" stays together.
- fact-lines-too-long: closed. On widescreen the fact lines are 41 to 45 characters per line, and "take." is no longer alone on its line.
- empty-bottom-third: open. On desktop and widescreen the content still ends at about y=537, and nothing answers the Pricing or "Shops using it" links.

**New problems.** None. The fixes added no new element: the Sign in change removed a filled button, and the copy change added no made-up facts.

**What would move it most**
1. The till line and the missing comparison. Location: the "Works with your till" fact line and the page as a whole. An owner whose till or card reader is not named will assume it is not supported, and nothing tells them how Shelfmark beats walking the shelves on Monday or reading the till's own sales report. Fix: the maker names the supported tills or card readers, and adds one line that compares Shelfmark with the owner's current routine. The maker must supply both facts. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
2. Nothing follows up the nav links. Location: the empty area below the fact lines. The bottom third of the desktop screen is blank, and a visitor who wonders about price or about other shops has to click away to find out. Fix: add a short pricing and shops section below the fact lines, using pricing and shop facts that the maker supplies. Taste. Viewports: desktop, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- Type sizes 16 and 14 px: keep 16 for body, and either take the table and date text down to 13 px or put it at 16 and set it apart by color, so the two levels read as clearly different. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
- Tablet fact lines: the second line runs 76 characters across 600 px, and "they happen." and "they take." sit as short last lines. Cap the width of the fact lines at about 34em on tablet. Viewports: tablet.
- Phone table: "Notes from the Ferry" and "The Glass Orchard" wrap to two lines. Give the Title column more width, for example by shortening "Sold this week" to "Sold" with the week shown in the table heading. Viewports: phone.

**What's working.**
- One rust accent, used only on the trial button. The call to action is clear at once in every viewport.
- The "Reorder this week" table with real-looking titles is concrete proof of what the product does. It is far better than a stock illustration.
- The phone stack order (headline, paragraph, trial, secondary button, table, fact lines) follows the reading order of the desktop layout. Nothing is lost or reordered.

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.

1	**First read.** The eye lands on the headline "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks". It then drops to the rust "Start a 30-day trial" button and crosses to the "Reorder this week" table. The page reads as a calm, plain product page for an independent bookshop's stock tool: warm off-white, one rust accent, and a real-looking table as proof. On tablet and phone everything stacks in one column in a sensible order: headline, paragraph, buttons, table, then the three fact lines. Nothing scrolls sideways.
2	
3	**What it's for.** It gets an independent bookshop owner to start a 30-day trial of Shelfmark, the stock-counting and reorder tool.
4	
5	**Verdict.** The fixes worked. The page now reflows on narrow screens, the trial is the one strong button, and the hero holds together on widescreen. What still stands between the page and a sign-up is copy only the maker can supply: which tills it works with, how it compares with the owner's Monday routine, and a section that answers the Pricing and "Shops using it" links.
6	
7	**Finding status**
8	- no-reflow-narrow-screens: closed. page_width is 390 on the phone and 768 on the tablet, and the phone h1 is 3 lines at 18 characters per line. The content is in one column and each button is on one line.
9	- sign-in-outshouts-trial: closed. In all viewports, Sign in is a plain nav link (weight 500, #2a2622), and "Start a 30-day trial" is the only filled button (white on #8a3b24, 7.69:1).
10	- copy-misses-fit-for-this-shop: open. The returns line now has a verb and speaks to the owner ("Tracks your returns. You see which unsold copies are due back, and when."). The till line still names no tills or card readers, and the page still has no comparison with what the owner does now.
11	- widescreen-hero-gap: closed. The h1 right edge is at x=984 and the table text starts at x=1075, about 91 px apart, inside the check's 200 px. The content is capped at 384 to 1536.
12	- faint-table-headers: closed. The headers and "Mon 9 June" measure 7.43:1, and violations is empty in all viewports.
13	- too-many-close-type-sizes: open, but only just. type_sizes is now 40 (32 on phone), 20, 16, 14, which meets the target of one body size and one small size. But 16 and 14 are exactly 2 px apart, which the "within 2 px" check catches.
14	- headline-lone-word: closed. On desktop and widescreen the headline is 2 lines and breaks after "shelves", so "before a customer asks" stays together.
15	- fact-lines-too-long: closed. On widescreen the fact lines are 41 to 45 characters per line, and "take." is no longer alone on its line.
16	- empty-bottom-third: open. On desktop and widescreen the content still ends at about y=537, and nothing answers the Pricing or "Shops using it" links.
17	
18	**New problems.** None. The fixes added no new element: the Sign in change removed a filled button, and the copy change added no made-up facts.
19	
20	**What would move it most**
21	1. The till line and the missing comparison. Location: the "Works with your till" fact line and the page as a whole. An owner whose till or card reader is not named will assume it is not supported, and nothing tells them how Shelfmark beats walking the shelves on Monday or reading the till's own sales report. Fix: the maker names the supported tills or card readers, and adds one line that compares Shelfmark with the owner's current routine. The maker must supply both facts. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
22	2. Nothing follows up the nav links. Location: the empty area below the fact lines. The bottom third of the desktop screen is blank, and a visitor who wonders about price or about other shops has to click away to find out. Fix: add a short pricing and shops section below the fact lines, using pricing and shop facts that the maker supplies. Taste. Viewports: desktop, widescreen.
23	
24	**Smaller things.**
25	- Type sizes 16 and 14 px: keep 16 for body, and either take the table and date text down to 13 px or put it at 16 and set it apart by color, so the two levels read as clearly different. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
26	- Tablet fact lines: the second line runs 76 characters across 600 px, and "they happen." and "they take." sit as short last lines. Cap the width of the fact lines at about 34em on tablet. Viewports: tablet.
27	- Phone table: "Notes from the Ferry" and "The Glass Orchard" wrap to two lines. Give the Title column more width, for example by shortening "Sold this week" to "Sold" with the week shown in the table heading. Viewports: phone.
28	
29	**What's working.**
30	- One rust accent, used only on the trial button. The call to action is clear at once in every viewport.
31	- The "Reorder this week" table with real-looking titles is concrete proof of what the product does. It is far better than a stock illustration.
32	- The phone stack order (headline, paragraph, trial, secondary button, table, fact lines) follows the reading order of the desktop layout. Nothing is lost or reordered.

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and the fix added no template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but the element the fix added is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the after image has and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background, as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. A new element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and the element the fix added is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.
62

summary:
**First read.** The eye lands on the headline "Know what is on your shelves before a customer asks". It goes next to the brown "Start a 30-day trial" button, then over to the "Reorder this week" table, which is the proof that the headline is true. It reads as a calm, plain landing page for a bookshop stock tool, and it feels honest and quiet. On desktop and widescreen, the content stops at about y=530, so the bottom third of the screen is empty and the page feels unfinished. On phone and tablet, the table stacks under the hero and the three fact lines stack below it, so the page reads as one column and the empty space goes away.

**What it's for.** It gets an independent bookshop owner to start a 30-day trial of Shelfmark. This is my assumption, taken from the work order and the primary button.

**Verdict.** The fixes made the type and the phone table tidier, but they did not change what the page tells an owner. The biggest thing still in the way is the "Works with your till" line, which names no till or card reader. An owner cannot tell whether their own till is supported, and that line needs facts that only the maker has.

**Finding status**
- till-line-and-comparison: open. The line still says "Works with your till. Sales come in from the shop's card reader as they happen." It names no tills, and no line compares Shelfmark with what the owner does now. It is the same at all four viewports.
- nothing-follows-nav-links: open. Content still ends at about y=530 of 800 on desktop and y=530 of 1080 on widescreen. Nothing on the page answers the Pricing or "Shops using it" links.
- type-sizes-16-and-14: closed. type_sizes is now 40/20/16/13 on desktop, tablet and widescreen, and 32/20/16/13 on the phone. The smallest gap is 3 px, and the table and date text read as a clear second level.
- tablet-fact-lines-too-wide: open. The measure is met: the lines are 544 px wide, with 66, 69 and 62 characters per line. But "they happen." and "and when." now sit as short last lines. The third line ("and when.") used to fit on one line in the before image.
- phone-table-title-wraps: closed. "Notes from the Ferry" and "The Glass Orchard" each measure 1 line. The column heading "Sold this week" became "Sold", and the card heading "Reorder this week" still gives the week.

**New problems.** On the tablet, the third fact line now wraps and leaves "and when." alone on its last line. Before the fix it was one line.

**What would move it most**
1. The till line names no tills (the "Works with your till" fact line, all viewports). An owner whose till or card reader is not named assumes it is not supported. Nothing on the page tells them why this beats walking the shelves on Monday or reading the till's own sales report. The maker should name the supported tills or card readers, and add one line that compares Shelfmark with what the owner does now. Only the maker has these facts, so do not invent them. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
2. Nothing answers the Pricing and "Shops using it" links (the empty area below the fact lines). The bottom third of the screen is blank on desktop and widescreen, and a visitor who wants to know the price has to click away. Add a short pricing and shops section below the fact lines, with pricing and shop facts that the maker supplies. Taste. Viewports: desktop, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- Tablet fact lines: "they happen." and "and when." sit alone on their last lines. Narrow the lines a little more, to about 32em, or let them run to the 600 px width of the table above them so they rebalance. Then check that no line ends with one or two words. Viewports: tablet.

**What's working.**
- The phone table now has five rows of equal height. With "Sold" as the column heading, the Title column has room, and the table reads as one even list.
- At 13 px with muted heading color, the table and date text read as a clear second level under the 16 px body text, and the contrast stays high (15.01:1 for the cells, 7.43:1 for the headings).
- The single brown primary button is still the only strong color on the page. Nothing added in this round competes with it.
